newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: South Africa details requirements for Telkom bidding.
newsitem.headline: South Africa details requirements for Telkom bidding.

text.p: Price, delivery and training will be the three key elements of bids expected by the end of January for up to 30 percent of South Africa's state-owned Telkom corporation, Minister Jay Naidoo said on Tuesday.

Naidoo, Minister of Posts, Telecommunications and Broadcasting, on Monday shortlisted Germany's Deutsche Telekom, France Telecom, Telekom Malaysia and South Western Bell of the United States as potential "strategic equity partners" for Telkom.

The partial sale of Telkom is crucial to a privatisation programme which is a key element in South African Finance Minister Trevor Manuel's strategy for growth, employment and redistribution, known as GEAR.
Some privatisation proceeds will be used to cut South Africa's debt. But telecommunications analysts expect most of the proceeds of the deal to be applied to improving service.
South Africa is likely to become only the second country in Africa after Guinea to accept a private partner into its fixed-line telecommunications industry.

Shola Taylor, Africa head of the London-based INMARSAT telecommunications cooperative, told Reuters recently that Cape Verde, Congo and Ivory Coast also were seeking strategic investors in their state telecommunications companies while Ghana and Uganda were planning a second fixed operator.
Taylor said that with fewer telephones than the city of Tokyo, the African continent offered the biggest growth market for telecommunications.

Naidoo did not comment on Tuesday on the cash price he hoped to fetch, but he has said previously that the sale, premised on a guaranteed fixed-wire telephony monopoly of four to six years, should raise five to six billion rand ($1.1-1.3 billion).
He told reporters he had a formula, which he was not willing to disclose, for the valuation of non-cash contributions.
"There is a weighting, but the most important elements would be financial, human resource development and rollout. They are the three most important issues for me," he said.
Telecommunications spokesman Connie Malusi said Telkom was committed to deliver two million new telephone lines and to upgrade a further one million existing lines in five years.
South Africa's parliament is about to adopt a draft law setting up an independent Telecommunications Regulatory Authority and a fund for the extension of telephone services to remote areas.

Pointing out that Telekom Malaysia and South Western Bell had entered the race together, Naidoo said he expected the four finalists to explore consortium bids that would exploit their relative strengths to maximum advantage.
British Telecommunications, Italy's Stet Spa, KPN of the Netherlands and Telia of Sweden have dropped out of the bidding in the last month.
"The bottom line still remains a 20 to 30 percent stake in Telkom...depending on the proposals coming from the potential partners," Naidoo said.
The government began talks with labour and black business last Sunday on an additional 10 percent stake reserved for a black economic empowerment programme.

Naidoo said factors that would influence final negotiations in the first quarter of 1997 would range from the ability to deliver telephone services to remote schools and clinics to the potential for cable television and video services.

Human resource development, including the transfer of skills to existing Telkom staff and potential for affirmative action for blacks disadvantaged under white rule would weigh heavily in negotiations.
